Identiﬁcation of the bovine HSL gene expression proﬁles and its association
with fatty acid composition and fat deposition traits
Xibi Fang1, Zhihui Zhao1, Ping Jiang, Haibin Yu, Hang Xiao, Runjun Yang⁎
College of Animal Science, Jilin University, No.5333 Xi'an Road, Changchun 130062, PR China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
HSL
Lipometabolism
Gene promoter
Beef cattle
Fatty acid composition
A B S T R A C T
Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) is an intracellular neutral lipase capable of hydrolysing a variety of esters and is
considered to be a candidate gene aﬀecting fat deposition traits. Gene expression proﬁles of HSL were analysed
in various adipose tissues of cattle, and the eﬀect of HSL on lipid metabolism genes was analysed by a PCR array.
Novel polymorphisms were identiﬁed within the HSL regulatory domain by sequencing, and the relationship
between HSL variants and fat deposition traits was analysed. HSL mRNA was highly expressed in the
subcutaneous and visceral fat of cattle. CPT1B/CPT1C and other lipocatabolic genes were upregulated, and
lipogenesis-related genes (FASN, LPL and ACOT12) were downregulated by HSL overexpression in BFFs. Five
novel variants in the HSL functional domain were signiﬁcantly associated with fat deposition traits, including
FCR, LBT, MFW and fatty acid composition. HSL plays a pivotal role in the regulation of lipolysis and fatty acid
biosynthesis in beef cattle.
1. Introduction
Beef provides important nutrients to the human diet, including B
vitamins, minerals such as iron and essential fatty acids (FAs)
(Pereira & Vicente, 2013; Williams, 2007). Cattle meat traits, especially
marbling and FA composition, are important factors aﬀecting meat
quality and are thus important in the beef industry (Laborde, Mandell,
Tosh, Wilton, & Buchanan-Smith, 2001). Due to recent advancements in
molecular genetics, it is now possible to identify DNA polymorphisms
that aﬀect traits of interest in livestock, which can lead to a better
understanding of the genes that contribute to variations in carcass and
meat quality traits in cattle, such as the dressed weight, fat colour score,
intramuscular fat level, and FA composition (Islam et al., 2009).
The hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) gene, which contains 9 exons, is
located on bovine chromosome 18. HSL is responsible for the hydrolysis
of the ﬁrst FA from a triacylglycerol (TAG) stored in adipose tissue and
thus the release of free FAs (FFAs) and is an important enzyme involved
in lipid metabolism. HSL is a multifunctional enzyme with high
expression
levels
in
both
intra-
and
intermuscular
fat
tissue
(Haemmerle, Zimmermann, & Zechner, 2003), but low expression levels
in adrenal gland, ovary, testis, heart, and skeletal muscle tissues (Wang
et al., 2004). Studies of overweight and obese men and women
identiﬁed
two
SNPs
in
the
promoter
region
and
17948C > T
(rs1206034) in intron 2 in the HSL gene and demonstrated that they
are correlated with plasma lipids and anthropometric and glucose-
related phenotypes (Qi et al., 2004). HSL is also considered to be a
candidate gene aﬀecting meat quality traits, and various HSL SNPs have
been reported to be correlated with carcass and meat quality traits, such
as the pH value, dressing percentage, net meat rate, and FA composition
(Fang et al., 2014; Goszczynski et al., 2014). In addition, Yonezawa
reported that saturated FAs (SFAs) could upregulate HSL mRNA in a
time- and concentration-dependent manner in bovine mammary epithe-
lial cells (Yonezawa, Haga, Kobayashi, Katoh, & Obara, 2008). We
speculate that some FAs may inﬂuence HSL expression or activity.
However, the 5′-terminal sequence of HSL has not been extensively
studied, and the molecular mechanisms by which HSL regulates meat
FA composition remain unclear. The present study characterized HSL
mRNA expression levels in diﬀerent tissues and analysed the association
between SNPs in the 5′-terminal sequence of HSL and fat deposition and
meat quality traits such as fat colour score, back fat thickness and FA
composition in longissimus dorsi muscle. In addition, HSL was over-
expressed in bovine foetal ﬁbroblasts (BFFs) to identify genes involved
in the regulation of lipid and FA metabolism pathways. The results of
this study lay the foundation for further study of the function of HSL in

2. Materials and methods
2.1. Ethics statement
All animal experiments in this study strictly abided by the ordinance
for the care and use of laboratory animals by the Jilin University
Animal Care and Use Committee (permit number: SYXK (Ji) 2012-
0010/0011).
2.2. Experimental materials
2.2.1. Animal cell line
BFFs were provided by Professor Lichun Zhang from the animal
biotechnology laboratory of Jilin Academy of Agricultural Science.
2.2.2. Blood and tissue samples
Blood samples (10 mL each) were collected from the jugular vein
with anticoagulant (acid citrate dextrose, ACD) and shipped back to the
laboratory at 4 °C. All blood samples were stored at −70 °C until
further analysis. Heart, liver, spleen, kidney, rumen, reticulum, petal
stomach, abomasum, large intestine, small intestine, longissimus dorsi
muscle, subcutaneous fat, omental fat and kidney fat tissues were
collected from three adult Chinese Simmental steers (Changchun,
China).
2.2.3. Animals
One hundred thirty-ﬁve Chinese Simmental steers (28 months old)
were provided by the Inner Mongolian Baolongshan cattle farm
(Tongliao, China) and were randomly selected from the oﬀspring of a
Simmental population of approximately 1000 female cows and 21 bulls.
2.2.4. Trait analysis
The carcasses were stored in refrigerated rooms at temperatures
between 0 and 4 °C for 24 h. The meat traits were then measured based
on the GB/T17238-1998 cutting standard for fresh and chilled beef in
China (China Standard Publishing House). The day after slaughter, a
block of steaks corresponding to the 12th and 13th ribs were removed
from the cold carcasses and kept at −20 °C until they were thawed for
FA composition analysis (Monziols, Bonneau, Davenel, & Kouba, 2007).
The intramuscular FA contents were extracted according to an AOAC
protocol (1992) and expressed as g/100 g fresh tissue. Analytical
determinations were performed at the Meat Laboratory of the Chinese
Academy of Agricultural Sciences. Marbling and other carcass and meat
quality traits were measured as described in our previous study (Fang
et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2017).
2.3. RNA extraction and real-time quantitative ampliﬁcation
Total RNA from three cattle was extracted using RNAiso Plus
(Takara Bio Inc., Dalian, China), and cDNA synthesis was performed
using a PrimeScript™RT Reagent Kit with gDNA Eraser (Takara Bio
Inc., Dalian, China) according to the manufacturer's protocol. Real-time
polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analyses were performed on a
PCRmax Eco 48 machine (PCRmax, UK) in a 10 μL reaction volume
including 5.0 μL of 2 × SYBR® Premix Ex Taq™(Tli RNaseH Plus)
(Takara Bio Inc., Dalian, China), 0.2 μL of forward and reverse primers
(10 μM), 1.0 μL of template cDNA, and 4.6 μL of nuclease-free water.
The real-time PCR conditions were as follows: 50 °C for 5 min; 95 °C for
5 min; and 40 cycles of 95 °C for 10 s and 59 °C for 30 s. The β-actin
gene was used as the internal reference gene (Table 1), and relative
expression levels were determined using the 2−△△Ct method.
2.4. Construction of the pBI-CMV3-bHSL vector and transfection of BFFs
A fragment containing the ORF of HSL was obtained by PCR, and
the plasmid pBI-CMV3 (Clontech, Beijing, China) was selected for HSL
overexpression. A map of pBI-CMV3 is shown in Fig. 2A. FuGene® HD
transfection reagent (cat. E2311, Promega, USA) was used to transi-
ently transfect BFFs with pBI-CMV3-bHSL and pBI-CMV3, and the cells
were collected for total RNA extraction 48 h after transfection.
2.5. Lipid and FA metabolism RT2 Proﬁler PCR array
Total RNA was extracted using an RNeasy Plus Universal Mini Kit
(Qiagen, Germany). After cDNA was synthesized from 2.0 μg of total
RNA using an RT2 First Strand Kit (Qiagen, Germany), quantitative PCR
was performed on an Mx3005p system (Agilent Stratagene, USA). The
transcript levels of genes involved in lipid and FA metabolism pathways
were analysed using a Custom RT2 Proﬁler PCR Array (CAPB13622A,
Qiagen) according to the manufacturer's protocol. We chose three
diﬀerent housekeeping genes, β-actin (ACTB), glyceraldehyde-3-phos-
phate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) and TATA-binding protein (TBP), as
internal controls, using the average geometric mean of their Ct values.
2.6. PCR ampliﬁcation, SNP detection and genotyping
DNA was extracted from eucocyte of cattle whole blood (10 mL per
each cattle) with a blood DNA extraction kit (Tiangen, Beijing, China)
according to the manufacturer's protocol. The purity and concentration
of the genomic DNA were determined using a NanoDrop ND-2000
ultraviolet spectrophotometer (Thermo). The quality of the genomic
DNA preparations was also veriﬁed by agarose gel electrophoresis.
Genomic DNA with an absorbance at OD260nm/OD280nm ≥1.80 and no
RNA or protein in the agarose gel was used as a template.
According to the 5′-terminal sequence and mRNA of the bovine HSL
gene in GenBank, primers (Table 1) were designed using Primer
Premier 6.0 (Premier Biosoft International, Canada) and synthesized
by GENEWIZ, Inc. (Suzhou, China). The 5′-terminal sequence of the
bovine HSL gene (AC_000175.1; −13,091 bp to −10,533 bp) was
ampliﬁed by PCR in a 50 μL reaction volume including 25.0 μL of
2 × Taq PCR Master Mix (Tiangen, Beijing), 1.0 μL of forward and
reverse primers (10 μM), 2.0 μL of template DNA (25 ng/μL), and
21.0 μL of nuclease free H2O. The PCR conditions were as follows:
95 °C for 5 min; 30 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s, 57 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for
1 min 30 s; and a ﬁnal 10 min extension at 72 °C. The PCR products
(50.0 μL) were run on agarose gels and puriﬁed using a DNA gel
puriﬁcation kit according to the manufacturer's instructions.
The puriﬁed PCR products were submitted to GENEWIZ, Inc.
(Suzhou, China) for DNA sequencing. The target peaks in the sequen-
cing chromatographs obtained for Chinese Simmental steers were

2.7. Statistical analysis
The expected heterozygote (He) frequency, observed heterozygote
(Ho) frequency, and Fis level were calculated using the Genepop website
to measure the genetic variation of a population. The polymorphism
information component (PIC) was calculated according to Botstein's
methods (Botstein, White, Skolnick, & Davis, 1980). Haplotype linkage
analysis was performed using HaploView 4.2 software (Daly Lab, USA),
and the SNPs with a minor allele frequency (MAF) < 1% were excluded
from this analysis. The transcription factor binding sites (TFBSs) in the
HSL gene sequence from −13,091 bp to −10,533 bp were predicted
using the PROMO website (http://alggen.lsi.upc.es/cgi-bin/promo_v3/
promo/promoinit.cgi?dirDB = TF_8.3). Associations between the SNPs
in the HSL gene 5′-terminal sequence and carcass and meat quality traits
were analysed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) using SPSS 13.0
for Windows, and p < 0.05 was deﬁned as statistically signiﬁcant. Real-
time PCR results are presented as the means ± SEM. The statistical
signiﬁcance of diﬀerences between groups was analysed by one-way
ANOVA using the GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad Software, San
Diego, CA, USA). Gene expression data were analysed by RT2 Proﬁler
PCR Array data analysis online software (https://www.qiagen.com/cn/
shop-old/data-interpretation-systems/bioinformatics/geneglobe-data-an
alysis-center/). Cells transfected with pBI-CMV3 were used as a control
group. The gene expression in the HSL overexpression group (cells
transfected with pBI-CMV3-bHSL) is presented as relative change
compared to the control group. p < 0.05 was deﬁned as statistically
signiﬁcant.
3. Results
3.1. HSL gene expression proﬁles in various adipose tissues of Chinese
Simmental steers
The HSL gene is widely expressed in various tissues, with high
expression levels in subcutaneous fat, kidney fat and omental fat but
low expression levels in the lung, spleen, omasum, kidney, rumen,
abomasum, and intestine in beef cattle, suggesting that HSL mRNA
expression pattern in cattle is consistent with that in human and mouse.
Subcutaneous fat had the highest expression level of HSL mRNA, while
the spleen had the lowest. The expression of HSL in all tissues in our
study (except adipose tissue) was signiﬁcantly diﬀerent from that in
subcutaneous fat, kidney fat and omental fat (p < 0.01). In addition,
the expression levels in the liver, lung, spleen, kidney, omasum,
abomasum, rumen and large intestine was signiﬁcantly diﬀerent from
that in longissimus dorsi muscle (p < 0.05). Interestingly, signiﬁcantly
diﬀerent levels of HSL mRNA were observed among three kinds of
adipose tissue (Fig. 1, p < 0.01).
3.2. Regulation of lipid metabolism-related genes by HSL overexpression
To study the function of HSL, we constructed the vector pBI-CMV3-
bHSL. Its map and digestion results are shown in Fig. 2A. To investigate
the eﬀect of HSL overexpression on mRNA expression, HSL mRNA was
analysed by real-time q-PCR. The mRNA expression of HSL in the pBI-
CMV3-bHSL-transfected group was signiﬁcantly increased compared to
that in the control group (Fig. 2B, p < 0.05). Meanwhile, the mRNA
expression of lipoprotein lipase (LPL), peroxisome proliferator-acti-
vated receptor gamma (PPARγ) and other related genes interact with
HSL in lipid metabolism pathways was signiﬁcantly reduced in the pBI-
CMV3-bHSL-transfected
group
compared
with the
control
group
(Fig. 2C, p < 0.05). These preliminary results showed that lipogenesis
genes were signiﬁcantly decreased upon HSL overexpression.
To further investigate the regulation of lipid metabolism-related
factors by the HSL gene in BFFs, the eﬀect of HSL on lipid metabolism
genes was analysed by a PCR array. The fold-change results of genes in
lipid and FA metabolism pathways are summarized in Table 2. Our data
suggested that increased HSL expression led to the upregulation of 62
genes, including carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1C (CPT1C), carnitine
palmitoyltransferase-1B
(CPT1B),
and
fatty
acid
binding
protein
2
(FABP2), while 15 genes were downregulated, including acyl-CoA
thioesterase 12 (ACOT12), fatty acid synthase (FASN), LPL and PPARγ
(Table 2). The enzyme encoded by the FASN gene is a multifunctional
protein, and its main function is to catalyse the synthesis of palmitate
from acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA during FA biosynthesis when the
FASN gene is activated by sterol regulatory element-binding protein
(SREBP). By contrast, CPT1C and CPT1B encode diﬀerent isoforms of a
member of the choline acetyltransferase family. These isoforms regulate
the β-oxidation and transport of long-chain FAs in mitochondria.
CPT1C/CPT1B plays roles in the regulation of mitochondrial transmem-
brane transport and the FA catabolic process. HSL overexpression
promotes the hydrolysis of triglycerides into FAs and glycerol, the
transport of large amounts of FAs into mitochondria and the β-
oxidation process. Therefore, the levels of CPT1C and CPT1B, which
regulate FA catabolism, were signiﬁcantly increased. Our data revealed
that HSL inﬂuences FA composition, especially SFAs, monounsaturated
FAs (MUFAs) and total FAs, by regulating genes in FA metabolism
pathways.
3.3. Detection of polymorphisms in the regulatory domain of the HSL gene
and genotyping
We next screened the SNPs in a key functional domain of the bovine
HSL gene in a Chinese Simmental cattle population. Based on the
sequencing results and the sequencing chromatographs of the PCR
products,
ﬁve
SNPs,
c.-11,470C > T,
c.-11,646 T > C,
c.-
12,253 G > A, c.-12,425 T > C and c.-12,465 T > C, were identiﬁed
in the 5′-terminal sequence of the HSL gene in a population of Chinese
Simmental steers (Fig. 3). For c.-11,470C > T, c.-11,646C > T, c.-
12,425 T > C and c.-12,465 T > C, the CC, CT, and TT genotypes
were observed in the Chinese Simmental steer population, with CC
being the dominant genotype. In addition, the C allele frequencies of
the 4 SNPs in the experimental population were much higher than those
of the T allele. For c.-12,253 G > A, GG, GA and AA genotypes were
detected, and the G allele was dominant. The locations, allele frequen-
cies and genotype frequencies of the 5 SNPs in Chinese Simmental
steers are summarized in Table 3.

given SNP site detected in a population, which serves as both the unit of

polymorphism. It is generally believed that a population with a
heterozygosity score exceeding 0.5 has not been exposed to high

The Ho values of the experimental population were between 0.331
and 0.395, and the He value was close to the Ho value. The hetero-
zygosities of all 5 SNPs in the 5′-terminal sequence were < 0.5,
suggesting that this particular population was not very genetically
diverse. The PICs of the 5 SNPs, which ranged from 0.30 to 0.32,
suggested intermediate polymorphism within the population, according
to the PIC value classiﬁcation (PIC value < 0.25, low polymorphism;
0.25 < PIC value < 0.5, intermediate polymorphism; and PIC va-
lue > 0.5, high polymorphism). Overall, these data indicate that the
HSL 5′-terminal sequence in the analysed population exhibits inter-
mediate genetic diversity, as shown in Table 3.
3.4. Association analyses of HSL polymorphisms with fat deposition, FA
composition and meat quality traits
These analyses revealed that the 5 SNPs in the 5′-terminal sequence
of the HSL gene were signiﬁcantly associated with carcass and meat
quality traits. At c.-11,470 T > C, the dressing percentage of TT
individuals was signiﬁcantly higher than that of CC individuals
(p < 0.05). At c.-11,646 T > C, the mesenteric fat weight of CC
individuals was higher than that of TT individuals, and the omental
fat weight (OFW) and kidney fat weight (KFW) of CC individuals were
higher than those of TC individuals (p < 0.05). At c.-12253A > G,
the mesenteric fat weights of GG and GA individuals were higher than
that of AA individuals (p < 0.05). At c.-12,425 T > C and c.-
12,465 T > C, the dressing percentage and net meat rate of CC
individuals were higher than those of CT individuals, and the mesen-
teric fat weights of CC and CT individuals were higher than that of TT
individuals (p < 0.05). Interestingly, all 5 SNPs were signiﬁcantly
associated with carcass fat coverage rate (FCR) and live backfat
thickness. The carcass FCRs of CC and TC individuals were higher than
those of TT individuals at c.-11470C > T, c.-11,646C > T, c.-
124,253 T > C and c.-12,465 T > C, whereas at c.-12,253 A > G,
the rates of GG and GA individuals were higher than those of AA
individuals. The live backfat thicknesses (LBTs) of CC individuals were

dorsi muscle of TC and AG individuals were higher than those of CC and

12,425 T > C, the longissimus dorsi muscle FA content, including
hexadecanoic acid, palmitoleic acid, heptadecenoic acid, oleic acid and
arachidonic acid, diﬀered signiﬁcantly between CC and CT individuals
(p < 0.05). At c.-12,465 T > C, the FA content in longissimus dorsi
muscle, including myristic acid, hexadecanoic acid, palmitoleic acid,
heptadecenoic acid and oleic acid, diﬀered signiﬁcantly between CC
and CT individuals (p < 0.05). In addition, the hexadecanoic acid and
heptadecenoic acid contents in longissimus dorsi muscle of TC indivi-
duals were signiﬁcantly higher than those of CC individuals at c.-
11,646C > T in the Chinese Simmental cattle population (p < 0.01,

3.6. Prediction of potential TFBSs in 5′-terminal sequences of the HSL gene
Putative TFBSs in wild-type and SNP-containing sequences were
predicted by PROMO. The c.-12,465 T > C mutation led to an addi-
tional TF ZF5 binding site and the deletion of two TFBSs (activating
protein-2αA and LVc). c.-12,425 T > C led to the elimination of
binding sites for LIM homeobox 1 (LIM1) and CCAAT/enhancer binding
protein alpha (C/EBPα). c.-12253A > G and c.-11,646 T > C caused
the elimination of binding sites for TBP and C/EBPα. In addition, c.-
11,470 T > C eliminated binding sites for high-mobility group protein
(HMG, I (Y)), POU class 1 homeobox 1 (POU1F1) and CCAAT/enhancer
binding protein delta (C/EBPδ) but added a binding site for Fanconi
anaemia complementation group B (FACB). The details of the TFBSs in
the 5′-terminal sequences are summarized in Fig. 5. The introduction of
SNPs into the 5′-terminal sequence could potentially alter the transcrip-
tion eﬃciency and cause transcriptional defects, leading to the up- or
downregulation of gene expression and aﬀecting biological functions.
The SNPs detected in the 5′-terminal sequence (−13,091 bp to
−10,533 bp) of HSL aﬀected TFBSs in the Chinese Simmental cattle
and might thus be partially responsible for individuals with a hetero-
zygous genotype having a higher LDM FA content than individuals with
the homozygous genotype, especially for hexadecanoic acid, palmito-
leic acid, heptadecanoic acid, and oleic acid. Two alleles in the 5′-
terminal sequence could have more TFBSs, increasing the activation
eﬃciency of HSL transcription and leading to high HSL expression
levels and elevated lipid hydrolysis, resulting in increased FFA release
(Fig. 5).

4. Discussion
HSL is an intracellular neutral lipase that is capable of hydrolysing
TAGs, diacylglycerols, monoacylglycerols, and cholesteryl esters as well
as other lipid- and water-soluble substrates (Kraemer & Shen, 2002).
The HSL protein contains three domains: an N-terminus involved in
protein-protein interactions and lipid binding, the catalytic domain,
and a regulatory domain containing multiple phosphorylation sites. The
coordination of functions in these three domains is thought to modulate
HSL activity (Cornaciu et al., 2011). The C-terminus is composed of
structural α/β hydrolase folds, which are common in many lipases and
esterases. Within this region is a common catalytic motif found in
lipases. Site-directed mutagenesis experiments have demonstrated that
the presence of the serine situated in this motif is critical to HSL enzyme
function. Within the regulatory domain, phosphorylation at up to four
serine residues may enhance lipolysis and, importantly, allow HSL to
translocate from the cytosol to lipid droplets during stimulated
lipolysis. In addition to being responsible for lipid binding, the N-
terminus interacts directly with fatty acid binding protein 4 (FABP4),
which is believed to act as an intracellular chaperone for FAs. The role
of FABP4 in lipolysis is not fully understood, but its interaction with
HSL has been shown to enhance lipolytic activity in vitro (Smith,
Thompson, Sanders, & Bernlohr, 2007). However, in this study, HSL
overexpression did not signiﬁcantly alter the expression level of FABP4,
indicating that during lipolysis, FABP4 can enhance HSL enzymatic
activity, as mentioned above, but HSL cannot regulate the expression
level of FABP4.
The transcription factor AP-2 alpha A (TFAP-2αA) has been shown
to play a critical role in regulating gene expression during early
development, apoptosis and cell-cycle control and may also be involved
in tumourigenesis (Hilger-Eversheim, Moser, Schorle, & Buettner, 2000;
Huang et al., 2016). In the present study, individuals with the T allele of
c.-12,465 T > C gained additional binding sites for AP-2αA and LVc,
which led to higher FA contents, dressing percentage and net meat rate
(p < 0.05) but lower mesenteric fat weight, KFW, LBT and living QIB
(p < 0.05). The newly added AP-2αA binding site in the 5′-terminal
sequence might also contribute to the changes in the HSL expression
level. Similarly, the higher FA content, dressing percentage and net

Interestingly, FA has been shown to regulate HMGA1 expression

The expression of genes involved in lipid metabolism regulation was
signiﬁcantly altered in BFFs upon HSL gene overexpression. These
genes include FABP2, CPT1C, solute carrier family 27 member 6
(SLC27A6), CPT1B, peroxisomal trans-2-enoyl-CoA reductase (PECR)
and 3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase 2 (BDH2), which are involved in
FA metabolism and are primarily responsible for FA synthesis and
transport (Chirala, Huang, Jayakumar, Sakai, & Wakil, 1997; Kaikaus,
Bass, & Ockner,
1990;

2003;
Storch & Thumser, 2000). In addition, polymorphisms in FASN showed
putative associations with FA traits in a population of Japanese Wagyu
(Abe et al., 2009; Hayakawa et al., 2015). However, only the CPT1C
gene exhibited a change in expression of > 2-fold. CPT1 is the rate-
limiting enzyme in FA β-oxidation, with three paralogous genes
(CPT1A, B, and C) in mammals, and regulates the entry of long-chain
FAs into mitochondria (Bonnefont et al., 2004). The increased tran-
scriptional level of CPT1B and CPT1C may aﬀect long-chain FA
transport and metabolism, thus altering the FA content. The primary
action attributed to HSL is hydrolysis of stored TAGs in adipose tissue,
i.e., lipolysis.
We speculate that mutations in HSL could aﬀect its transcriptional
level by altering the binding of diﬀerent transcription factors, subse-
quently regulating the expression of genes involved in lipid and FA
metabolism pathways in beef cattle. In the future, we will focus on the
eﬀect of SNPs in the 5′-terminal sequence on transcription factor
binding and their inﬂuence on HSL expression regulation. Given our
better understanding of the mechanism and genetic variants of HSL and
their correlation with meat quality, the HSL gene could be applied in
MAS programmes to adapt bovine meat quality according to consumer
and market demands.
5. Conclusions
Overall, in the present study, the bovine HSL gene was highly
expressed in the subcutaneous and visceral fat of beef cattle. Upon HSL
overexpression in BFFs, CPT1C, CPT1B, FABP2, BDH2, PECR and other
lipocatabolic genes were upregulated, and lipogenesis-related genes
(FASN, LPL, ACOT12 and PPARγ) were downregulated. A correlation
analysis also showed that ﬁve novel SNPs in the functional domain of
HSL were signiﬁcantly associated with fat deposition traits, including
FCR, LBT, MFW, and FA composition, including SFA, MUFA and PUFA
contents. HSL plays a pivotal role in the regulation of lipolysis and FA
biosynthesis, and mutations in its 5′-terminal sequence could aﬀect the
recruitment of TFs to the HSL regulatory region, further inﬂuencing
expression levels and altering traits by regulating lipometabolic-related
genes. HSL could serve as a useful molecular marker in MAS in the beef
cattle breeding process.
